questions.question_text: Explain why enzyme activity increases as temperature rises to an optimum and then decreases rapidly above the optimum.

required_mark_points.description: Rising temperature increases kinetic energy of enzyme and substrate molecules.
required_mark_points.improvement_instruction: State that rising temperature increases molecular kinetic energy.

required_mark_points.description: Molecules move faster and collide more frequently.
required_mark_points.improvement_instruction: Link increased kinetic energy to more frequent collisions.

required_mark_points.description: More enzyme-substrate complexes form, increasing reaction rate up to the optimum.
accepted_phrases: reaction rate increases up to the optimum
required_mark_points.improvement_instruction: Explain how collisions increase complex formation and rate.

required_mark_points.description: Above the optimum, bonds maintaining the enzyme's tertiary structure are disrupted.
accepted_phrases: bonds in the tertiary structure break
required_mark_points.improvement_instruction: Identify disruption of bonds maintaining tertiary structure.

required_mark_points.description: The active site changes shape and is no longer complementary to the substrate.
accepted_phrases: no longer complementary to the substrate
required_mark_points.improvement_instruction: State how denaturation changes the active site.

required_mark_points.description: Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, so activity decreases rapidly.
required_mark_points.improvement_instruction: Finish the causal chain by linking active-site change to reduced complex formation.

contradictions.message: Low temperature normally slows activity but does not usually denature the enzyme.

contradictions.phrase: active site becomes more complementary above the optimum
contradictions.message: Above the optimum, denaturation reduces complementarity.

misconceptions.message: Use the scientific term denatured rather than saying the enzyme is killed.

questions.model_answer: As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy, move faster and collide more frequently. More enzyme-substrate complexes form, so the reaction rate increases up to the optimum. Above the optimum, bonds maintaining the enzyme's tertiary structure are disrupted. The active site changes shape and is no longer complementary to the substrate, so fewer complexes form and activity decreases rapidly.
